question: Can neural-network generalization be explained by making each labeled training input a local extremum of every one-vs-rest output function, and can such networks be trained without backpropagation by solving layerwise systems of equations?

key_findings.claim: The paper recasts a sigmoid multiclass network as a collection of one-vs-rest scalar functions and defines an ideal classifier by placing positive examples at their global maxima and negative examples at their global minima.
key_findings.evidence: The output vector is decomposed into one scalar sigmoid head per class. The proposed ideal termination rule assigns the selected class output to 1 and all others to 0, while a weakened rule merely separates them around 0.5.

key_findings.claim: For one input, the paper derives a homogeneous linear system in the final-layer weights whose solutions make all first input derivatives of an output vanish.
key_findings.evidence: For each scalar output, setting every partial derivative with respect to the input to zero gives m linear equations in the last hidden layer's width. The paper argues that width greater than input dimension guarantees infinitely many solutions for this stationarity system.

key_findings.claim: The proposed EI training procedure stacks stationarity constraints over all training inputs and progressively introduces earlier-layer weights when the last-layer system is insufficient.
key_findings.evidence: Section 3.3 defines L(n,-,Phi) by concatenating one system per sample. Algorithm 1 then moves backward from the output, solves L(u,-,Phi), calls an unspecified Polarize operation to choose a class-separating particular solution, and expands the network if no such solution is found.

key_findings.claim: The rank argument proves only stationarity, not that a training input is a maximum or minimum and not that it has the desired class value.
key_findings.evidence: Vanishing first derivatives are necessary but not sufficient for a local extremum in multiple dimensions; the paper itself later acknowledges saddle points. Moreover, the all-zero final-layer weights satisfy every homogeneous stationarity equation but yield no class separation. Algorithm 1 excludes the zero solution operationally, yet no theorem establishes a nonzero solution satisfying the polarization and label constraints.

key_findings.claim: The core training algorithm is not executable as presented because its decisive polarization subroutine is enumeration over a continuous solution family with no search rule or complexity bound.
key_findings.evidence: Section 4 says polarization selects a particular solution that both flips extrema into the correct orientation and expands their values, but Section 6.1 explicitly states that no efficient algorithm has been proposed and that enumeration is the only method. Without polarization, the output of the linear-system step is not a classifier.

key_findings.claim: The earlier-layer reduction is not justified by treating products of weights as independent variables in a linear system.
key_findings.evidence: At L(n-1,-), the paper suggests regarding products such as w[n] times w[n-1] as single unknowns and applying homogeneous linear-equation methods. Arbitrary solutions in the lifted product variables need not factor consistently into shared layer matrices, so this substitution does not establish existence or provide recovery of valid network parameters.

anchors.section: 3.3, proposed linearization of the nonlinear system

key_findings.claim: The claims about generalization, vanishing or exploding gradients, and overfitting are deductions from the proposed geometry rather than validated consequences.
key_findings.evidence: The paper contains no implemented EI experiment, benchmark, numerical example, convergence result, generalization bound, or comparison with backpropagation. It equates unsolvability with an infinite solution and with gradient explosion, treats unused early weights as gradient vanishing, and interprets inability to add samples as overfitting, but does not derive those equivalences from the loss-gradient dynamics of backpropagation.

key_findings.claim: The formal scope is much narrower than modern neural-network practice.
key_findings.evidence: The derivation removes biases, uses fully connected networks with sigmoid hidden and output units, treats only supervised classification, and depends on differentiability with respect to a fixed-dimensional input. The discussion leaves softmax, ReLU, saddle classification, and an implementable polarization method open.

method.core_idea: Impose first-order stationarity of each class-output function at every training input, solve the resulting output-weight equations, and introduce earlier layers only when the current system cannot produce a label-oriented particular solution.
method.mechanism: For a bias-free sigmoid multilayer perceptron, recursively expand input derivatives of each scalar output. Stack their zero-derivative constraints across samples into L(u,-,Phi), solve a homogeneous system from the last layer backward, then polarize a solution so each labeled input becomes a high maximum for its class and a low minimum for other classes. A neighborhood heuristic relaxes exact stationarity to cluster representatives.
assumptions: Inputs live in a continuous fixed-dimensional Euclidean space and the network is differentiable with respect to every input coordinate.
A first-order stationary point can be selected and oriented as the required class maximum or minimum.
Solutions of lifted equations in products of layer weights can be factored into consistent network matrices.
Enumeration or a future polarization algorithm can find a useful particular solution at practical cost.
Training-sample extrema, rather than behavior between or outside samples, determine generalization.

techniques.role: Turns zero input gradients at training examples into algebraic fitting constraints.
Uses the null space of last-layer derivative coefficients as the proposed alternative to gradient descent.
Introduces products involving earlier weights when final-layer degrees of freedom are insufficient.
Names the missing selection step intended to turn stationary solutions into correctly oriented class extrema.
Reduces the number of exact constraints by training cluster-center samples and checking nearby members.

limitations: Author-stated: no efficient polarization algorithm is supplied; enumeration is the only proposed route.
Author-stated: the derivation does not cover softmax fully, nondifferentiable ReLU networks, or the distinction between extrema and saddles.
Reviewer-identified: there is no empirical evaluation, executable implementation, convergence analysis, complexity analysis, or generalization test.
Reviewer-identified: zero-gradient constraints admit trivial constant outputs and do not encode class values or curvature.
Reviewer-identified: lifting products of weights as independent variables omits factorization constraints.
failure_modes: The null space may contain only solutions that are constant, saddle-producing, or incompatible with the desired labels.
Polarization can require an unbounded search through a continuous family and therefore fail computationally even when a mathematical solution exists.
A function can satisfy every training-point stationarity constraint yet behave arbitrarily between samples and generalize poorly.
Piecewise-linear activations, biases, convolutional parameter sharing, residual connections, and normalization break key simplifications in the derivation.
The lifted equations can return product values that cannot be factorized into a shared set of layer weights.
reusable_insights: Input-gradient constraints can be a diagnostic or regularizer even when they are insufficient as a complete training objective.
Any analytic alternative to backpropagation should separate existence of a stationary solution, recovery of parameters, label satisfaction, curvature, computational cost, and out-of-sample behavior.
Null-space degrees of freedom could initialize or constrain an optimizer, but require an explicit secondary objective to avoid trivial solutions.
Negative or incomplete algorithms are useful research objects when their missing subroutine is specified precisely enough to falsify.
open_questions: Can a tractable constrained optimizer find nontrivial null-space solutions that also satisfy output margins and Hessian-sign constraints?
What is the smallest counterexample where all proposed EI equations are solvable but no consistent weight factorization or class-polarized network exists?
Do input-stationarity regularizers improve robustness or instead worsen interpolation and adversarial gradients when added to ordinary loss training?
Can the neighborhood heuristic be given a Lipschitz or margin guarantee that relates cluster radius to classification error?
How does the cost of solving the stacked systems compare with reverse-mode differentiation at realistic widths and sample counts?

competitive_landscape.title: Explicit Computation of Input Weights in Extreme Learning Machines
competitive_landscape.difference: This work gives a concrete single-pass construction and solves output weights with a pseudoinverse for an extreme-learning-machine architecture; EI instead constrains input derivatives across deep sigmoid layers but does not provide a complete parameter-recovery algorithm.

competitive_landscape.title: Difference Target Propagation
competitive_landscape.difference: Difference target propagation sends corrected activation targets through learned inverse maps and reports benchmark results; EI proposes a global algebraic stationarity system and leaves its decisive solution-selection step unresolved.

competitive_landscape.title: Direct Feedback Alignment Provides Learning in Deep Neural Networks
competitive_landscape.difference: Direct feedback alignment retains iterative local weight updates using fixed random error projections and demonstrates learning in deep and convolutional networks; EI replaces error propagation with equation solving but supplies neither an executable polarization procedure nor empirical evidence.

competitive_landscape.title: NoProp: Training Neural Networks without Back-propagation or Forward-propagation
competitive_landscape.difference: NoProp trains blocks as local target-denoisers and validates the resulting algorithm on MNIST, CIFAR-10, and CIFAR-100; EI seeks exact training-input extrema through linear systems and remains a conceptual, unbenchmarked framework.

novelty_assessment.author_claim: The paper claims that neural-network generalization comes from dynamically mapping training data to function extrema and proposes EI as a fundamentally different, equation-solving alternative to backpropagation.
novelty_assessment.evidence: The novel construction is the stack of input-stationarity equations and a layerwise solve-and-polarize outline.
novelty_assessment.reviewer_inference: The extremum framing is unusual, but the paper establishes only a null-space condition for zero first derivatives in a simplified network. It neither proves extrema or generalization nor completes or evaluates the EI algorithm, so the supportable novelty is a speculative constraint formulation rather than a demonstrated learning method or explanation of neural networks.

reviewer_notes: Read end to end, including all derivations, Algorithm 1, deductions, stated open problems, and references. Competitor records were checked on primary arXiv/PMLR pages on 2026-08-23. Claims labeled reviewer inference identify algebraic gaps; they are not claims made by the author.
